sections.html:
Mandan faces Bismarck across the Missouri, at the east end of Morton County, and serves as the county seat. The 2020 census counted 24,206 residents and the estimate for July 1, 2025 is 25,061, enough for eighth place among North Dakota cities. Interstates 94 and 194 run through, and the ZIP code is 58554.

The town grew out of a railroad camp in 1878. Homes near the old center can be a century old, and newer subdivisions have far younger systems, so condition swings widely between neighboring streets. Inspectors spend the most time on wiring, plumbing and heat in the older blocks.

sections.h2: Winter wear and what inspectors check
sections.html:
Seasons here swing hard. January afternoons average about 22.5 degrees and nights about 2.7, which keeps a furnace running for months. Expect roof, heating and foundation to get the closest look from a buyer.

The city's building department treats furnace changeouts and water heater changeouts as permit jobs. If you swapped one out without a permit, the paperwork question will likely come up during inspection. Dig out receipts and permit records before listing.

Selling doesn't require a permit, but missing permits for past work tend to stall a Mandan deal once questions start. The Building Department (701-667-3230) wants a permit before work begins, noting that a construction record matters at sale, refinance or insurance time. The city's permit FAQ names these jobs:

  • any structural alteration, residential or commercial
  • residential construction over $2,000
  • window replacements that change the window size
  • any structure larger than 120 square feet
  • furnace changeouts, water heater changeouts and fireplace installs
  • water and sewer hookups

Painting, carpeting, tiling, countertops, fences up to 8.5 feet and swimming pools don't need one. A permit usually takes under an hour to issue, and inspections carry no extra charge. Verify a contractor's license with the state before paying for pre-sale repairs.

Cities bill nearby owners for public projects through special assessments, and any balance still owed stays with the property when it changes hands. Mandan uses assessments for street paving, water and sewer mains, sidewalks, curb and gutter, and also for weed cutting, snow removal and diseased tree removal.

On the city's special assessment page, water, sewer and street costs are generally spread over 15 years. Repairs to private water or sewer lines and tree removal are typically spread over five. Weed cutting and delinquent utility bills carry a 10 percent administrative fee. The city auditor certifies each year's installment to the county by November 1, and owners can pay without interest through February 15 of the following year.

  • Search an address or parcel on the city's Special Assessment Inquiry Dashboard. If the parcel doesn't appear, no specials are on it.
  • Call 701-667-3271 for payoff figures, or visit the Auditor's Office at 205 2nd Avenue NW.
  • For rural parcels outside city limits, Morton County handles balances at 701-667-3326.

Ask for a payoff figure first. That sum is taken from your proceeds when the sale closes.

sections.h2: Property tax dates and how the tax is figured
sections.html:
A Morton County bill starts with the assessor's market-based value. Half of it becomes assessed value, and a home's taxable value comes to 4.5 percent of the full figure. Mills levied by the city, school district and other local bodies are then applied. The State Tax Commissioner's residential property tax page explains each step.

StepTiming or contact in Morton County
Statements mailedEach December, and by statute by December 26
Discount5 percent off consolidated tax if paid by February 15; a postmark counts
Payable without penaltyUntil March 1
Questions on valueMorton County Tax Equalization Office, 701-667-3325
AppealsState Property Tax division, 701-328-3127, with a questionnaire and evidence

A bill lost in the mail is still owed. The state's residential page lists credits for a primary residence and for homestead, and if you still qualify, claim one before you sell.

sections.h2: Before you list: a short checklist
sections.html:
A little preparation keeps a Mandan sale from stalling at the last step. Work through these in order.

  • Look up your parcel on the special assessment dashboard, and call the Auditor's Office if anything shows.
  • Find your latest tax statement and confirm whether the February 15 discount or the March 1 deadline is still ahead.
  • Gather permit records for any furnace, water heater, addition or structural work, and note anything done without one.
  • Locate any radon test results and, if you belong to an association, its documents and fee information.
  • Check that the name and mailing address on your deed are correct for the Recorder.

With those in hand, a title company can quote payoffs quickly and a buyer, cash or financed, has fewer reasons to pause.

Before a buyer signs final acceptance, the seller of a one-to-four unit home gives a written statement of material facts (N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1). Estate fiduciaries, foreclosure sales and close-family transfers are carved out.

  • Radon: section 47-10-02.2 has you state in writing what you know about radon levels and pass along any test or mitigation records.
  • Associations: section 47-10-02.3 sets ten days after signing for association documents and fee details.
  • Deeds: section 47-10-07 puts the mailing address of every grantee on the deed.

Your deed goes to the Morton County Recorder, whose land records feed the tax rolls. Owners can sign up there for a free Property Fraud Alert that flags any new recorded document. Read the statutes in the legislature's Title 47 chapter 10.

A Mandan homeowner can go with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer for the house as it stands. The timelines and costs differ.

Listing opens the door to the most buyers, though it means showings, repair requests and a loan that hinges on an appraisal. A cash buyer has no lender, and takes the property in its current state, handy when there's deferred maintenance, a tenant or an addition built without a permit. Compare offers by what lands in your pocket once assessments, taxes and liens are paid.

Cash Home Buyers doesn't promise a price here. Send us a Mandan address and we'll show how an offer is built. Saying no costs you nothing.

The process is brief. You describe the house, we explain the offer, and if you agree a title company prepares the closing papers, settles assessments and unpaid taxes out of the proceeds, and files the deed with the county. No showings, no lender appraisal and no repair haggling.

faqs.q: Is Mandan the county seat of Morton County?
faqs.a: Yes, since 1881. The courthouse, Recorder, Treasurer and Tax Equalization offices all sit in town, so recording and tax questions stay local.

faqs.q: When are Mandan property taxes due?
faqs.a: Statements go out each December. Pay by February 15 for a 5 percent discount on the consolidated tax (a postmark counts), or by March 1 to avoid a penalty.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed to replace a furnace or water heater in Mandan?
faqs.a: Yes, both are on the city's permit list. For any other project, call the Building Department at 701-667-3230.

faqs.q: Who pays special assessments when a Mandan house is sold?
faqs.a: The contract decides, so get it in writing. The debt belongs to the parcel. The Auditor's Office at 701-667-3271 can give you a payoff figure before you accept an offer.

faqs.q: Must I give a buyer a disclosure statement?
faqs.a: In most sales of homes with up to four units, yes. The written statement is required by N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1, with a radon statement added by 47-10-02.2. Estate fiduciaries, foreclosures and some family transfers skip the main form.
